title: You thought evil, God turned it to good (Genesis 50:15–21)
hookLine: Joseph's last word to his brothers on their fear

cards: Jacob lives out his days in Egypt, and dies there. His sons carry him home to Canaan and bury him in the cave Abraham bought. And the moment the funeral is over, the brothers panic.
Their father was the reason Joseph was kind to them, they think. What if Joseph was only waiting? So they send a message: before he died, our father told us to tell you, please forgive your brothers.
Then they come themselves, fall down before him, and say: we are your servants. Whether Jacob ever said that, the text doesn't tell us. Only that Joseph, hearing it, weeps.

teach.b: Then his answer. Don't be afraid, he tells them.

And then: "You thought evil against me: but God turned it into good," to save many people. He doesn't say it wasn't evil, or that God made them do it. He says two things happened at once: their plan, and God's.

teach.h: PROVIDENCE: TO SEE AHEAD, AND PROVIDE.
teach.b: Today's word for that is providence, from the Latin providere, to see ahead and so to provide. The Catechism says God guides all creation toward its goal, and is never the author of evil, yet can draw good even out of it.
For an example, it uses this very story: Joseph telling his brothers it wasn't they who sent him, but God. Then it goes further, to the cross.
The worst thing human beings ever did, it says, God turned into the greatest good. Now look back over Genesis. It opened with in the beginning: light, then six days and a rest.
Adamah. A serpent, and a question, ayekkah. A brother who asked if he was his brother's keeper.

Noah building, a bow in the clouds, Babel. Abraham told to go forth, counting stars, and on a mountain saying God will provide. And it ends here, with a brother answering that old question about keepers.

teach.h: FROM A GARDEN TO A COFFIN IN EGYPT.
teach.b: Genesis begins with a garden and ends with a coffin in Egypt, and a promise that God will come for his people.

how: The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches divine providence in its section on God the Creator (paragraphs 302–314), and uses Joseph's words to his brothers as an example of God drawing good out of evil.

o: luck that happens to turn out well in the end
God's guiding care, drawing good even from evil
a reward God gives to people who forgive

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: Latin: to see ahead, to provide
God's plan, at the same time

s: Joseph tells his brothers what they did wasn't really evil
he calls it evil. he says God turned it into good.
the Catechism teaches that God is the author of evil
it says God is never the cause of moral evil, but can draw good out of it.
the Catechism uses Joseph's story to explain providence
it quotes Joseph: it wasn't you who sent me here, but God.

games.q: you're Joseph. your father is dead, and your brothers are on the floor in front of you, offering to be your slaves. you have all the power. what do you say?
o: don't be afraid. you thought evil, but God turned it into good.
say nothing, and let them wait.
games.why: he weeps, tells them not to fear, and promises to feed them and their children. the brothers expected revenge; they got providence.

practice: Think of something that hurt, a loss, a betrayal, a door that closed, and without pretending it was good, look gently at what grew around it afterward: a friend you wouldn't have met, something you understand now, a kindness you can offer because you know that pain.
If nothing has grown yet, that's honest too. If you pray, thank God for one good thing without calling the wound good; if you don't, simply notice both, side by side.

wordCard.voice: Providence. God's seeing ahead and guiding all things, never causing evil, yet able to draw good out of it. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: foresight, provision, from providere, to see ahead. the Church's word for God's guiding care.

carryVoice: Your line: god turned it to good. Not that it was good, but that good was drawn from it. Genesis, done.
